title: Peace officers failed to check on man who died in police custody: ASIRT
article: Community peace officers failed to properly check on a man who died in Edmonton police custody more than two years ago, Alberta's police watchdog says.

In March 2020, police arrested a 53-year-old man on warrants near 108 Avenue and 101 Street and placed him in the holding cells at the Downtown division headquarters, where he was found unresponsive the following day. He died despite efforts by emergency medical services to treat him on the scene.

Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) investigated the death and released a decision Wednesday that found community peace officers on duty at the time did not follow Edmonton Police Service (EPS) policy on checking detainees, and two in particular appear to have tried to hide that fact.
Since ASIRT's mandate does not extend to peace officers, "any further action regarding them is the responsibility of EPS," the decision said.
Edmonton Police Service was not able to comment on the incident and the decision before deadline.

After interviewing police as well as civilian witnesses and analyzing video of the cell where the detainee died, ASIRT said the man was placed in a cell at 11:44 p.m. on March 15, 2020, after a paramedic found him alert and responsive with no injuries.

Another person, identified only as a male, was placed in the same cell the next morning shortly after 7 a.m., not long before video appears to show the two of them consuming drugs and the original detainee proceeded to lie on a bench and face the wall.
While police may conduct a cursory pat down or frisk, they may not conduct a strip search as a matter of practice or routine, ASIRT said.

"In the absence of articulable grounds, police are not entitled to conduct a strip search," ASIRT said. "Sadly, this means that, on occasion, a person may be able to successfully maintain possession of controlled substances on their person when they are detained in custody."
At 8:13 a.m. the detainee appeared to spasm, and then moved slightly for the next two minutes. The cell video shows him making no more movements after 8:15 a.m.

Between 8:30 a.m. and 1:42 p.m., the video then shows peace officers walking by the cell about every 10 minutes and looking in as they passed before eventually entering the cell at 12:14 p.m. and again about 75 minutes later.

At 1:37 p.m. the second detainee checked on the first before moving away to stand by the cell door. Five minutes later, a peace officer entered, appeared to notice something wrong with the first detainee and left before returning with a paramedic and another peace officer to perform CPR and administer naloxone on the motionless man until emergency medical services arrived.
Following a March 17, 2020, autopsy, a medical examiner found that the man died of fentanyl toxicity.

EPS policy regarding detainees states that walk-around physical checks must be performed every 15 minutes and arousal checks must be performed every hour, ASIRT said, and the latter involves waking and speaking with a detainee to confirm they are responsive an not in need of medical assistance. While the arousal check can be performed from outside the cell, a peace officer must enter the cell if there is no response.

ASIRT reviewed interviews EPS detectives conducted with three peace officers, one of whom said they were conducting arousal checks every 40 minutes, which involved ensuring the detainee was breathing. The same peace officer said he performed a check before lunch and made eye contact with the detainee.
A second peace officer said he performed an arousal check at 12:40 p.m. and did not remember having any concerns.
"Video shows peace officers on duty that day had not conducted a single arousal check on (the detainee) between 8:30 a.m. and 1:42 p.m.," ASIRT said.

While it's not clear whether the detainee went into medical distress after lying down or in the hours that followed, there is a lack of clarity due to peace officers not conducting hourly arousal checks in accordance with EPS policy.

ASIRT investigates Alberta police incidents involving misconduct, serious injury and death. Since no police officers were involved with the detainee after his arrest, there is no grounds to believe any officer committed an offence, the watchdog said.
